grammar.md:
**Commands: the imperative.** To tell one person to do something, use the verb stem with **-ε**; to tell several people, **-ετε**:

| | one person | several |
|---|---|---|
| λέγω | λέγ**ε** *speak!* | λέγ**ετε** |
| ἀκούω | ἄκου**ε** *listen!* | ἀκού**ετε** |
| μένω | μέν**ε** *stay!* | μέν**ετε** |
| φυλάττω | φύλαττ**ε** | φυλάττ**ετε** |
| σπεύδω | σπεῦδ**ε** | σπεύδ**ετε** |

The plural imperative looks exactly like 'you (all) do': *ἀκούετε* is both 'you are listening' and 'listen!'. Context (and the tone of voice) decides. The accent of the imperative goes as far back as it can: ἄκουε, φύλαττε; a verb of two syllables keeps it on the first: λέγε, μένε. A long vowel before a short final syllable takes the circumflex: σπεῦδε, καθεῦδε.

**Don't!** Prohibitions use **μή**, not οὐ: *μὴ τρέχε* 'don't run', *μὴ λέγετε* 'don't talk'. οὐ says what is not the case (*οὐ τρέχει* 'he isn't running'); μή says what should not happen.

**Greetings.** *χαῖρε* (to one), *χαίρετε* (to several) literally means 'be glad!' and serves for hello and goodbye.

**Calling someone: the vocative.** When you address a person, the noun takes the **vocative** case, usually with **ὦ** in front. Second-declension nouns in -ος change to **-ε**: ὦ πάππ**ε**, ὦ Λάβρ**ε**, ὦ Σύρ**ε**, ὦ δοῦλ**ε**. First-declension nouns keep their nominative form (ὦ Θρᾷττα, ὦ κόρη); names in -ας shorten to -α (ὦ Κλεινία). Third-declension names drop their ending: ὦ Λύσι, ὦ Ἐλπί, ὦ Χρυσί, ὦ παῖ, ὦ Ζεῦ, ὦ Προμηθεῦ. In the plural the vocative is the same as the nominative: ὦ παῖδες, ὦ δοῦλοι. The article is never used with a vocative.

**σύ with a command** adds emphasis or picks someone out: *σὺ δέ, ὦ Λάβρε, μὴ τρέχε* 'and you, Labros, don't run'.

culture.title: Prometheus, fire and the potters
culture.md: The oldest telling of the story is Hesiod's, around 700 BC: Prometheus tricks Zeus over the division of a sacrifice, Zeus hides fire from mortals, and Prometheus steals it back in a hollow fennel stalk. Zeus chains him to a rock and sends an eagle to eat his liver, which grows back each night; Heracles shoots the eagle and sets him free. Hesiod adds the sequel in which Zeus punishes humanity with Pandora and her jar, a πίθος, the huge storage vessel that potters like Ariston made. The tragedy *Prometheus Bound*, attributed to Aeschylus, was performed in Athens in the decades before our story. Athenians honoured Prometheus as a god of craft and fire alongside Hephaestus and Athena: his altar stood in the grove of the Academy outside the Dipylon gate, and at his festival, the Prometheia, runners carried torches lit at that altar in a relay through the Kerameikos into the city, straight past the potters' kilns. A kiln fired at 900 degrees or more for hours, and everything could crack or blister at the end; a short poem preserved with the Homeric hymns has a potter praying to Athena to hold her hand over the kiln and cursing the kiln-demons Smasher, Crasher and Shake-to-pieces. Children heard such stories at home long before they met Homer at school; Plato says it was mothers and nurses who told the μῦθοι, and a grandfather who had rowed at Salamis would have had plenty of his own.
